definition: ClearTalk is a controlled natural language—a kind of a formal language for expressing information that is designed to be both human-readable (being based on English) and easily processed by a computer.
details: Anyone who can read English can immediately read ClearTalk, and the people who write ClearTalk learn to write it while using it. The ClearTalk system itself does most of the training through use: the restrictions are shown by menus and templates and are enforced by immediate syntactic checks. By consistently using ClearTalk for its output, a system reinforces the acceptable syntactic forms. It is used by CODE4, the experimental knowledge management software Ikarus, and by a knowledge base management system Fact Guru. ClearTalk is easily readable by most people who can read English, and requires very little training to write. Databases of information have been written using ClearTalk by a 9-year old human. More than 25,000 facts have been encoded in ClearTalk. ClearTalk allows varying degrees of formality or specificity, allowing the author to choose to leave or remove ambiguity. ClearTalk was created in 1988 and fell out of use about 2006. It is the oldest controlled natural language with a formal representation.

explainer.lead: ClearTalk turns knowledge into English-like statements that people can read and software can process. Menus, templates, and immediate checks help writers use its accepted forms without learning a completely separate-looking notation.

tiers.eli5: ClearTalk is like writing notes with a set of sentence building blocks instead of using any English wording you like. A computer can understand those notes more easily, while people can still read them almost like ordinary English. Menus and quick checks show which blocks fit as you write.
tiers.practitioner: ClearTalk is applied by composing facts through its menus and templates, with immediate syntactic checks enforcing permitted forms. It has been used in CODE4, Ikarus, and Fact Guru. The main pitfall is assuming that English-looking output is unrestricted English or necessarily unambiguous: authors can choose how much ambiguity to remove.
tiers.paperLevel: ClearTalk is an English-based controlled natural language with a formal representation, designed for both human readability and computer processing. It permits varying degrees of formality and specificity, so an author may retain or remove ambiguity rather than every statement being fully unambiguous. Created in 1988 and falling out of use around 2006, it is the oldest controlled natural language with a formal representation.

explainer.example: A writer could enter “A cat is an animal.” The system would check that the sentence follows an allowed form and, once accepted, represent it as a fact that software can process.

explainer.intuition: Ordinary English is easy for people but often difficult for software to interpret reliably. ClearTalk narrows the allowed wording while preserving an English-like appearance, creating a middle ground between readable prose and formal notation.
howItWorks: Start with the knowledge the author wants to record.
Express it in English-like sentences using permitted forms.
Use menus and templates to discover those forms.
Apply immediate syntactic checks as the author writes.
Use ClearTalk consistently for system output to reinforce accepted syntax.
explainer.whyItMatters: ClearTalk lets people contribute structured knowledge without first mastering an unfamiliar formal language. More than 25,000 facts were encoded in it, including databases written by a nine-year-old.
misconceptions: It is not unrestricted English; its accepted syntactic forms are enforced.
English-like text is not automatically unambiguous, because authors choose the degree of formality and specificity.

diagram.caption: ClearTalk guides English-like writing through checks into facts used by knowledge systems.
